name: template-method
intent: Define the skeleton of an algorithm once, in a non-overridable operation, and let subclasses fill in the individually varying steps, so the order of the steps stays fixed while their behaviour varies.
problem: The same algorithm is repeated across several classes with only a few steps differing: each copy must be kept in sync by hand, a change to the shared part has to be applied everywhere, and one missed copy diverges silently.
context: Base classes and frameworks whose workflow is fixed while individual steps vary per implementation - import/export pipelines, request handling, test lifecycles, build stages, game turns - and where implementations arrive as subclasses of a base class or as conformances to an interface whose provided method carries the sequence.
benefits: The invariant part of the algorithm - the sequence, resource handling, the shared steps - is written once and reused by every variant instead of being copy-pasted into each of them.
A new variant is a new subclass that implements only the steps that differ, so the base class stays closed for modification (open/closed).
The order of steps is decided in one place, which lets the base class enforce pre- and post-conditions, locking, logging or transaction framing around every variant.
The extension points are explicit: primitive operations must be implemented, hooks may be overridden, and everything else is the base class's business.

Inversion of control is what makes a framework possible at all: the library owns the flow and calls the application's steps (the Hollywood principle) instead of requiring the application to call library functions in a prescribed order.
tradeoffs: The skeleton freezes the algorithm: a variant cannot change the order or skip a step, and a genuinely different flow means editing the base class rather than adding a subclass.
Fragile base class: the steps are an implicit contract, so renaming, splitting, reordering or removing one breaks existing subclasses - and no compiler checks the sequence, only the signatures.
Maintenance cost grows with the number of steps: the more primitive operations and hooks a base class declares, the harder the hierarchy is to read and the more work each new subclass is.
Liskov risk: a subclass may override an optional step to do nothing or weaken its default, so a subtype can quietly violate what callers expect from the base class.

The variation axis is static: behaviour is fixed at class-definition time (compile time in static languages), so it cannot be swapped per object at run time the way a composed strategy can, and combining two independent axes needs a second hierarchy.

It keeps inheritance as the extension mechanism with all the coupling that implies - one subclass per variant, all of them coupled to the base's protected surface, and subclass explosion when the steps vary independently.

participants.responsibility: Declares and implements the template method that fixes the order of the steps, provides the concrete operations every variant shares, and declares the primitive operations and hook operations that subclasses fill in.
An abstract step declared by the abstract class and implemented by each concrete class; it is required for the algorithm to be complete.
A step with a default (often empty) body at a deliberate extension point; a subclass may override it to extend the algorithm without being forced to.
Implements every primitive operation and overrides the hooks it cares about; it inherits the template method and must not restate it.

use_cases: Import/export and ETL pipelines where open, parse, validate, transform and write are fixed while the format-specific parsing and writing vary per concrete importer or exporter.

Framework and protocol lifecycles: servlet dispatch (HttpServlet.service calling doGet/doPost), test fixtures (setUp/runTest/tearDown), Android Activity lifecycle (onCreate/onStart/onResume), and Flask's full_dispatch_request (request_started → dispatch → response → teardown) all fix the sequence and leave the handler to the application.

Flutter StatefulWidget and React class-component lifecycles: the framework controls the sequence (initState/build/dispose in Flutter; componentDidMount/render/componentWillUnmount in React) while application code supplies the step implementations, making the lifecycle itself a template method.
Resource-lifecycle wrappers that acquire a resource, run subclass steps in between and then commit or release deterministically — locks, transactions, file streams, database sessions.

Algorithm skeletons parameterised by one operation: sorting (qsort's compar, Go's sort.Interface Len/Less/Swap) and traversal (iterate versus visit) fix the algorithm and take the comparison or visit step from the caller.
Document, report and code generation where the same assemble-render-emit flow is shared and each output format or target supplies its parts.
Game and simulation turns: the same turn order (collect, build, move, attack) is shared while each faction implements the steps.

State machines with fixed transition logic: the state handler base class defines enter/execute/exit and dispatches to concrete state implementations, enforcing that every state follows the same lifecycle.
Database migration frameworks (Flyway, Django migrations): the runner fixes discover → validate → apply → record while each migration supplies its own up/down SQL.
Build system task graphs (Gradle, Bazel): the task base class fixes inputs → execute → outputs caching while each tool supplies its own execution logic.
Python unittest framework: TestCase.run() is the template method that calls setUp() (hook), each test method, and tearDown() (hook), fixing the test lifecycle while test authors supply the steps.
Django class-based views: the as_view() class method and dispatch() method form a template method fixing the request-to-response pipeline while subclasses supply handler methods (get, post).
Data science preprocessing pipelines: a base DataProcessor abstract class defines clean/validate/transform/process with fixed ordering while each processor implements format-specific logic.

Netty's ByteToMessageDecoder: callDecode() fixes the decode loop - repeatedly invoking decode() while the input has readable bytes and progress is being made, guarding against mid-loop handler removal and stalled decodes - while each protocol subclass implements only the abstract decode() step.

Spring Framework's RdbmsOperation: the base compile() fixes the validate-then-compile flow and defers the operation-specific part to the abstract compileInternal() implemented by subclasses (SqlQuery, StoredProcedure), which then execute through a shared JdbcTemplate.

Java Collections skeletal implementations: java.util.AbstractList builds add(E), iteration and removal around the two steps size() and get(int) plus the optional add(int,E) - whose javadoc calls it a template method defaulting to UnsupportedOperationException - so a list subclass supplies only the storage steps.
avoid_when: The whole algorithm varies rather than individual steps: pass a strategy or a function and compose the behaviour instead of subclassing.
The variation must be selected or changed at run time per object: composition over inheritance.
Only one implementation exists, or the base class changes often: a plain method with private helpers or a composed collaborator is simpler and avoids the fragile-base-class problem.
The optional behaviours must be combined independently: pass collaborator objects, because a subclass can only cover one axis of variation.

The language cannot keep the skeleton non-overridable and untrusted third parties extend the base: prefer a non-virtual interface (wrapper plus hook) or plain composition so a subclass cannot bypass the invariant.
anti_patterns: Public virtual template method: the skeleton is offered as an extension point, so subclasses replace the algorithm instead of only its steps, which is the opposite of the pattern's rule.
Hook explosion: every line of the algorithm becomes a protected virtual step 'for flexibility', leaving no real skeleton and forcing subclasses to implement everything.
Inheritance as configuration: a subclass for every parameter combination, producing a combinatorial zoo instead of composing the differences.
Empty base class: the common class only declares steps and contains no shared work, so inheritance is used for reuse the algorithm does not justify.
Step names that encode mechanics (step1, phaseTwo) or leak the base class's internals, so subclass authors have to guess which members to override.
Constructor calling overridable steps: the subclass is not yet constructed when the step runs, so field initialisers and overridden behaviour are bypassed.
God base class: the abstract class accumulates shared logic across unrelated concerns because 'everything uses this skeleton', producing an unmaintainable monolith that every subclass depends on.
design_principles: Hollywood principle / inversion of control: the base class calls the subclass's steps, not the other way round - the property that makes a framework a framework.
Separate invariant from variant: the fixed part is written once and the varying parts are isolated in named operations (DRY applied to algorithms).
Open/closed principle: new variants arrive as new subclasses without editing the algorithm.
Liskov substitution as a design duty: subclasses may replace steps but must not weaken the contract of the operation they inherit.
Design the step set as deliberate API: primitive operations and hooks are the published extension surface, not incidental protected members.
best_practices: Make the skeleton non-overridable — non-virtual in C++, final in Java, sealed in C#, final-by-default in Kotlin, final func in Swift, @final in Python (type-checker enforced only) — and keep it free of step logic; external callers use only the template method.
Keep the step set small and each step narrow: primitive operations for what truly varies, concrete operations for what all variants share, hooks only where a default is meaningful.
Document the call order, mark required steps abstract so the compiler or type checker forces them, and give every hook an empty or sensible default.

Name hooks by intent (do_/on_ prefixes for actions/results, e.g., doConnect, onDataReceived), keep them out of the public API, and never call them from constructors, destructors or other published operations.
Expose step methods as protected, not public: external clients should interact only with the template method, not call steps directly.

Test the skeleton once with a recording subclass that asserts the step order, and test the steps individually with test doubles or friend-access where the language requires it; the contract is then verified for the whole family.
Prefer composition when the variation is a policy or must be swapped at runtime; keep inheritance for the case where the skeleton itself is the abstraction worth naming.

When steps need different parameters across variants, use a uniform step interface with ignored parameters rather than overload the template method signature; document which parameters are ignored per variant.

Limit inheritance depth: one level of concrete subclasses over the abstract base is ideal; multi-level chains (concrete → intermediate abstract → base) signal that a second axis of variation has entered and composition should be considered.
Add a hook as a no-op before and after each expensive or external-operation step so subclasses can log, instrument or cancel without overriding the step itself.
Version the step set: when a step is renamed or removed, treat it as a breaking API change that requires a migration guide and a deprecation period.
In Python, use abc.ABC with @abstractmethod for required steps; attempt to instantiate an incomplete subclass raises TypeError, surfacing contract violations early.

In Python, use @final from typing on the template method for static type-checker enforcement, and supplement with __init_subclass__ validation if runtime enforcement is required against determined mis-use.
In Python, avoid calling abstract or hook methods from __init__: defer execution to an explicit .run() or .execute() call so the object is fully constructed before the template method fires.
In Python, prefer None as a hook's default argument value rather than a mutable default to avoid shared state across instances; initialise state in __init__.

related_patterns_notes.state: a State machine's state handler often implements enter/execute/exit as a template method, fixing the lifecycle while concrete states supply the transition logic; differs in that State concentrates on the current-mode behaviour while Template Method concentrates on an algorithm skeleton.
related_patterns_notes.command: a Command's execute() is a single step, whereas Template Method fixes a sequence of steps; Template Method with a single abstract step is structurally equivalent to Command.
related_patterns_notes.observer: the observer's update() hook is a template method step; Template Method can frame an observee's notification sequence, but Observer focuses on one-to-many state propagation while Template Method focuses on algorithm structure.
